title: Nothing like Him
hook: there is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing (42:11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayat, signs in the horizons and in themselves, and your line was signs out there, signs in here. Which sign did you catch, outside or in? Today ends the week, and opens Surah Ash-Shura. Day five hundred sixty-seven.

Count the pairs in the room you're in. Two shoes. Two hands. Socks, earrings, chairs around a table. Look outside: male and female birds, day and night, hot and cold. Most things you can name have a match somewhere, a twin, a counterpart, something they're like. Try to name one thing that has no likeness anywhere. It's harder than it sounds. Surah Ash-Shura, verse eleven, sets up that exercise, then gives its answer.

Verse eleven begins with creation. The Originator of the heavens and the earth. He made for you mates from among yourselves, and for the cattle, mates. Pairs, everywhere, multiplying. Then, against all those pairs, the line. Pickthall: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." Laysa ka-mithlihi shay'. We met this verse on day two hundred forty-eight, for its last two names. Today, the first half. Look closely at the Arabic. Ka means like. Mithl also means like. Both are there: literally, there is nothing like His like. Grammarians have discussed why. Some say the doubled word is emphasis, like saying nothing, nothing at all, is like Him. Others read it as: there isn't even anything like something like Him. Either way, the sentence closes every door to comparison twice. Surah al-Ikhlas says it in one short line. Pickthall: "And there is none comparable unto Him." So everything in the world has a pair, and the One who made the pairs has none. Muslims make no pictures of God, and mosques are adorned with calligraphy and pattern instead. Muslim theologians have discussed at length how to speak about Allah at all. Different schools drew the lines in different places, with this verse in view. Then the verse does something gentle. Right after saying nothing is like Him, it says He hears and He sees. Beyond every picture, and still listening.

The practice: sit with what can't be pictured. Close your eyes. Notice how the mind reaches for an image whenever it thinks of anything: a face, a light, a shape. Let each image come, and gently set it down: not that, not that. Don't try to fill the space with something better. Just rest in the not-picturing. If you pray, you might rest in the verse: nothing is like Him, and He hears. The bell holds the time.
Ka-mithlihi, like His likeness, said twice in Ash-Shura's verse to close every door to comparing Allah with anything made in pairs. Today's word.

Your line: beyond every picture, still listening. Today, notice the pairs: shoes, hands, birds, days. Each one is a quiet reminder of the One who has none. Day five hundred sixty-seven, and the end of a week: Ghafir, the hidden believer, ud'uni, idfa', standing firm, the signs, and the One with no likeness.

howItsDone: Muslims do not make images of God; mosques are decorated with calligraphy and geometric pattern, and 42:11 and Surah al-Ikhlas are central to how Muslim theology speaks about Allah.

fork.setup: the verse has just described creation in pairs: mates for people, mates for cattle. what comes next?
options: and Allah too has a pair.
pairs are the secret of the world.
fork.reveal: nothing is like Him, and He is the Hearer, the Seer: everything has a pair, and its Maker has none.

original.note: Arabic: there is nothing like His likeness, with like said twice (ka, mithl).

trapdoor: what you thought: God is very great.
what it means: in a world where everything has a pair, Allah has no likeness at all, and still hears and sees.

what a scholar hears: the doubled comparison (ka + mithl) is read as emphasis or as negating even a likeness of a likeness; the verse anchors tanzih, while schools of kalam differed on reading the attributes.
